Auditing is a systematic evaluation of controls, policies, and procedures to determine effectiveness. You will see how internal audits support continuous improvement and how external audits provide objective assurance and certification. We will also look at practical activities: configuration audits that check system baselines, log and audit trail analysis to detect suspicious behavior, and the structured remediation of findings using a Plan of Action and Milestones. A common misconception is that passing an audit equals perfect security — instead, audits demonstrate adherence to standards at a moment in time and highlight areas that need ongoing management. By the end of this module you will be able to explain audit types, map controls to frameworks, perform simple configuration checks, and describe how to track remediation to closure.

screens.title: What is a Security Audit?
screens.narratorSegment: A security audit is a systematic evaluation of an organization's security controls, policies, and procedures to determine whether they are effective and properly implemented. At its core, an audit compares what is in place against what is required — whether by internal policy, an industry standard, or a regulator. A concrete example is checking whether servers enforce password aging and whether SSH root login is denied. Audits produce evidence: configuration snapshots, log extracts, and policy documents that prove controls exist and function. A common misconception is equating audit results with overall security: an audit shows adherence at a point in time but does not guarantee absence of vulnerabilities. Another misconception is thinking audits are only for compliance; they are also a tool for operational improvement because internal audits highlight process gaps before regulators find them. In practice, audits follow a repeatable pattern: scope the review, collect evidence, evaluate controls, report findings, and track remediation. For you as a practitioner, the most valuable outcome is an actionable set of findings with owners and deadlines, not just a pass or fail. As you review audit reports, ask whether the evidence shows sustained control operation or just one-time configuration changes.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.8 › What is a Security Audit?
Security Audit — Definition & Purpose
A structured review to compare actual control implementation against requirements, and to produce verifiable evidence.
Scope the review: systems, controls, timeframe.
Collect evidence: configs, logs, policies, interview notes.
Evaluate controls and report findings with risk ratings.
Concrete example
Verify SSH configuration and password policy: gather /etc/ssh/sshd_config and /etc/login.defs, compare values to baseline, and capture outputs as evidence.
Common misconception
Passing an audit snapshot does not mean continuous security. Audits are periodic checks; controls must be maintained and verified over time.
Key Takeaway

Audits produce traceable evidence that controls exist and operate, and they should drive remediation and continuous improvement.

screens.title: Internal vs External Audits
screens.narratorSegment: Internal and external audits serve related but different purposes. An internal audit is conducted by staff within the organization to identify risks, check operational controls, and drive continuous improvement. It tends to be more frequent and flexible in scope, focusing on process efficiency and internal policy compliance. An external audit is performed by an independent third party to provide objective assurance, certification, or regulatory evidence. External auditors follow defined standards and produce reports relied upon by regulators, customers, and partners. A concrete example: an internal security team may run quarterly configuration audits and adjust baselines, while an external auditor performs an annual certification review for ISO 27001 or a regulatory assessment for HIPAA. Misconceptions include assuming that internal audits replace external audits — they do not. Internal work reduces the risk of failures during external reviews, but external audits provide the independent attestation organizations often require. When planning audits, align internal audit findings to the external audit scope: document evidence, assign owners, and include remediation milestones so external reviews see a mature control environment rather than ad-hoc fixes. Ask yourself: does the evidence demonstrate sustained control operation or only a single point-in-time change?

screens.title: Compliance Frameworks Overview
screens.narratorSegment: Compliance frameworks provide structured approaches to identify and manage information security risk. Each framework serves different purposes. NIST Cybersecurity Framework is voluntary guidance organized into five core functions — Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, and Recover — and is useful for prioritizing improvements. ISO/IEC 27001 defines requirements for an information security management system and is the basis for certification to show an implemented, auditable program. GDPR and HIPAA are legal requirements for data protection in the EU and health data in the U. S., respectively; compliance means meeting specific privacy, protection, and retention rules. PCI DSS targets cardholder data environments and defines technical controls for payment processing. A concrete example: use NIST CSF to map gaps and prioritize mitigations, then adopt ISO 27001 to formalize the ISMS so you can produce certification evidence. A common misconception is treating frameworks as mutually exclusive; in practice they are complementary. Organizations often use NIST to structure risk management, ISO 27001 to show governance, and regulatory regimes like GDPR to define legal obligations. Effective auditors expect to see mapped controls, documented evidence, and how controls satisfy multiple frameworks where applicable.

screens.title: Configuration Audits and CIS Benchmarks
screens.narratorSegment: Configuration audits verify that systems match an approved secure baseline. Baselines provide explicit settings for operating systems, network devices, applications, and databases. Consensus baselines such as CIS Benchmarks give practical, vendor-agnostic guidance to harden systems. A configuration audit workflow typically includes selecting the baseline, scanning systems with automated tools, reviewing deviations, and recording evidence of remediation. For example, a baseline might require SSH root login to be disabled and password aging parameters to be set; an automated scanner detects deviations and generates a report. Relying exclusively on manual checks is a common mistake because human reviews are error-prone and inconsistent across many systems. Instead, use automation and configuration management tools to enforce and periodically check desired state. Another misconception is that baselines are one-size-fits-all; they must be adapted to organizational context and justified for deviations. The key practical skill is being able to run a configuration scan, interpret deviations, assign remediation, and capture the before-and-after evidence that an auditor will accept. This continuous loop — enforce, scan, remediate, and verify — is how organizations maintain secure configurations at scale. Configuration Audits and CIS Benchmarks means use baselines like cis benchmarks with automated scanning and enforcement to detect and remediate deviations consistently.. In practical terms, baselines, automated scans, and why consistent configs matter. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 8 › Chapter 8.8 › Configuration Audits
Audit Steps
  1. Select or adapt a baseline (e.g., CIS Benchmark).
  2. Run automated scans against targets.
  3. Review deviations and assign remediation.
  4. Verify remediation and collect evidence for auditors.
Why automation matters

Example checklist items

screens.title: Practical Configuration Checks (Linux)
screens.narratorSegment: This screen shows conceptual command checks you would use in a configuration audit on Linux hosts. The goal is to capture simple, verifiable outputs that demonstrate settings like password aging and SSH root login. For example, checking /etc/login. defs for PASS_MAX_DAYS, PASS_MIN_DAYS, and PASS_WARN_AGE shows whether password policies meet baseline requirements. A key example workflow is to run the grep commands, capture outputs to a file, and store that file as evidence. A common misconception is that running these commands proves continuous compliance; they only prove state at the capture time. Use automation to run these checks periodically and collect historical records. The code panel here is conceptual and meant for auditors: show the command, the expected secure output, and the captured evidence filename. When you prepare evidence for an auditor, include the command run, the timestamp, and the resulting output so the auditor can reproduce or validate the finding. content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.8 › Linux Config Checks
Conceptual Commands and Expected Output
# Example: Basic Linux configuration check (conceptual)
# Check for strong password policy in /etc/login.defs
grep -E "PASS_MAX_DAYS|PASS_MIN_DAYS|PASS_WARN_AGE" /etc/login.defs

# Check for SSH root login disabled in /etc/ssh/sshd_config
grep "PermitRootLogin" /etc/ssh/sshd_config
# Expected output: PermitRootLogin no

# Check for firewall status (example using firewalld)
sudo firewall-cmd --state
sudo firewall-cmd --list-all

# Capture outputs to evidence files with timestamps
# Example: /var/audit/evidence/ssh_check_2023-03-15.txt
What to record for auditors
  • Command executed and exact timestamp
  • Captured output saved as evidence file
  • Owner who ran the check and method used
Misconception check
A single successful check is not continuous proof. Automate scheduled scans and retain historical outputs to show sustained compliance.

screens.title: Automated Configuration Management vs Manual Checks
screens.narratorSegment: Manual configuration checks can work for small environments, but they quickly become unmanageable and inconsistent at scale. Automated configuration management uses tools to enforce a desired state, meaning systems are configured according to defined baselines and deviations are corrected automatically or flagged for remediation. Examples of automation include using configuration management platforms to push approved settings or using scanners that report drift and produce evidence for auditors. A practical contrast: a manual checker edits a single SSH configuration file and records the change, while an automated system enforces the setting across hundreds of hosts and re-applies it if drift occurs. The advantage for audits is clear — automation creates repeatable, timestamped evidence and reduces human error. A common misconception is that automation removes all oversight; it does not. You still need to review exceptions, document justified deviations, and ensure automation itself is auditable. For auditors, show automation run logs, policy definitions, and a history of enforcement actions to demonstrate control over configurations across time. Automated Configuration Management vs Manual Checks means automation enforces baselines, produces repeatable evidence, and reduces configuration drift compared to manual checks.. In practical terms, enforce desired state and reduce drift with automation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Manual Checks

  • Prone to human error and inconsistency
  • Hard to scale and to provide continuous evidence
Automated Management
  • Enforces desired state across many systems
  • Produces execution logs and history for audits
  • Enables periodic scanning and continuous compliance reporting

screens.title: Analyzing Audit Trails and Logs
screens.narratorSegment: Audit trails and logs are the historical record auditors and investigators use to understand what happened on systems. Logs from operating systems, applications, network devices, and security tools must be collected centrally, correlated, and retained according to policy. Effective log management lets you detect unauthorized access attempts, verify control operation, and reconstruct events during an incident. A concrete example: a policy requiring that all failed admin login attempts record the username and source IP can be validated by examining auth logs to see those fields are present. Centralized collection using a SIEM provides correlation and alerting, which is especially helpful when several sources are required to understand complex events. A common mistake is retaining logs only locally or for too short a period; this undermines both forensic analysis and compliance. To prepare for audits, ensure logs include required fields, are time-synchronized, are retained for the policy window, and that indexing or correlation rules exist to demonstrate detection capability. When you review logs, always verify the presence of essential fields and whether the logs were altered or truncated, because reliable logs are a core piece of audit evidence.

screens.title: Plan of Action and Milestones (POAM)
screens.narratorSegment: A Plan of Action and Milestones is a structured record used to track remediation of audit findings. When an auditor identifies a finding — for example, an unpatched vulnerability or a configuration deviation — the POAM records a clear description, the risk and impact, the owner responsible for remediation, target completion dates, and verification steps to confirm the fix. It acts as both a program management tool and audit evidence showing that issues are being treated as prioritized risks. A concrete example: an external audit finds an unpatched web server. The POAM entry lists the vulnerability, assigns the server owner, sets an action to apply the patch within a defined timeframe, notes compensating controls if needed, and defines a verification step such as a follow-up scan and evidence file. A common misconception is that a POAM is a formality; in reality, it is an accountability tool. Auditors will look for realistic milestones, assigned owners, and recorded verification demonstrating that each finding moved to closure. For security teams, a POAM is essential for turning audit results into measurable program improvement. Plan of Action and Milestones (POAM) means a poam turns findings into tracked remediation tasks with owners, milestones, and verification steps auditors can review.. In practical terms, tracking remediation from finding to verification. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Managing Audit Findings Effectively
screens.narratorSegment: Managing audit findings is more than recording them; it requires triage, ownership, prioritized remediation, and verification. Start by classifying findings by risk and compliance impact so the most critical items receive urgent attention. Assign each finding to a responsible owner who understands the technical fix and business impact. Define realistic milestones in the POAM and include verification steps such as rescans or test evidence. For communication, provide concise summaries to leadership and detailed remediation plans to implementers. A common mistake is closing findings without proper verification; always require evidence that the remediation worked and document the test. Another pitfall is letting low-priority items languish — they should still be tracked with owners and timelines. Concrete practices include weekly status updates for open POAM items, a suggested remediation owner and backup, and documented compensating controls if immediate remediation is impossible. The goal is auditable closure: evidence that the issue was fixed and verified. This disciplined approach turns audit activity into measurable reductions in organizational risk. screens.title: Simulated Log Analysis Exercise
screens.narratorSegment: In this hands-on exercise, you act as an auditor reviewing a simulated auth log for compliance with a policy: all failed administrative login attempts must be logged with username and source IP, and no administrative account should accept logins from external IP addresses. The simulated log includes several lines: a failed password for an invalid user with a public IP, an accepted root connection from an internal IP, a sudo event, and an accepted admin login from a public IP. First, check whether failed attempt entries include the username and source IP — the log shows both in the failed attempt, so that requirement is met. Second, look for administrative accounts logging in from external IPs — an accepted admin login from a public IP indicates a potential policy violation and must be flagged. A common misconception is to treat failed attempts as the only concern; successful administrative logins from unexpected source IPs are as important. Your auditor output should note which lines meet logging requirements and which indicate violations, assign an owner to investigate the external admin login, and create POAM entries to remediate access controls. This process turns logs into verifiable compliance evidence and operational actions.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn how organizations assess and prove their security controls through auditing and compliance testing. Auditing is a systematic evaluation of controls, policies, and procedures to determine effectiveness. Compliance testing verifies whether an organization meets legal, regulatory, or industry requirements such as ISO 27001, GDPR, HIPAA, or PCI DSS. You will see how internal audits support continuous improvement and how external audits provide objective assurance and certification. We will also look at practical activities: configuration audits that check system baselines, log and audit trail analysis to detect suspicious behavior, and the structured remediation of findings using a Plan of Action and Milestones. Understanding these topics matters because audits are both a technical check and a communication tool: they produce evidence that stakeholders, regulators, and partners rely on. A common misconception is that passing an audit equals perfect security — instead, audits demonstrate adherence to standards at a moment in time and highlight areas that need ongoing management. By the end of this module you will be able to explain audit types, map controls to frameworks, perform simple configuration checks, and describe how to track remediation to closure.

In this lesson you will build four measurable skills that map directly to real audit workflows. First, you will differentiate internal and external audits so you can choose the right review for risk reduction or certification. Second, you will explain major compliance frameworks like NIST CSF and ISO 27001 and map common controls to business requirements. Third, you will perform configuration audits using secure baselines so systems meet policy and reduce attack surface. Finally, you will analyze logs and manage audit findings with a Plan of Action and Milestones so remediation is tracked to completion. Each objective includes hands-on checks and examples. For instance, a configuration audit could include verifying SSH root login is disabled and that password aging is set, while log analysis exercises focus on whether failed admin login attempts include source IP and username. Understanding these tasks matters because auditors expect traceable evidence, and skilled practitioners both prevent incidents and prove compliance. As you learn, watch for a common misconception: meeting a checkbox on a framework is not the same as maintaining risk reduction — audits must be part of a continuous program with documented verification and remediation.

This second objectives screen clarifies the practical outcomes you should achieve. You will learn to assemble evidence sets that auditors accept: configuration snapshots, log exports, control matrices, and documented POAMs with owners and milestones. You will practice reading audit trails to spot unauthorized access or policy breaches and learn which log fields are essential — for example, username and source IP for failed administrative logins. You'll also gain the ability to interpret framework guidance: use NIST CSF to structure a program across Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, and Recover, and use ISO 27001 to demonstrate an implemented ISMS. Finally, you'll learn to prioritize remediation based on risk and compliance impact so your POAM entries include risk, owner, targeted completion, and verification steps. A common misconception to avoid is treating compliance solely as checkbox activity. Instead, think of audits as an evidence-producing practice that supports continuous security improvement. These skills let you both reduce risk and communicate compliance credibly to stakeholders.

A security audit is a systematic evaluation of an organization's security controls, policies, and procedures to determine whether they are effective and properly implemented. At its core, an audit compares what is in place against what is required — whether by internal policy, an industry standard, or a regulator. A concrete example is checking whether servers enforce password aging and whether SSH root login is denied. Audits produce evidence: configuration snapshots, log extracts, and policy documents that prove controls exist and function. A common misconception is equating audit results with overall security: an audit shows adherence at a point in time but does not guarantee absence of vulnerabilities. Another misconception is thinking audits are only for compliance; they are also a tool for operational improvement because internal audits highlight process gaps before regulators find them. In practice, audits follow a repeatable pattern: scope the review, collect evidence, evaluate controls, report findings, and track remediation. For you as a practitioner, the most valuable outcome is an actionable set of findings with owners and deadlines, not just a pass or fail. As you review audit reports, ask whether the evidence shows sustained control operation or just one-time configuration changes.

Internal and external audits serve related but different purposes. An internal audit is conducted by staff within the organization to identify risks, check operational controls, and drive continuous improvement. It tends to be more frequent and flexible in scope, focusing on process efficiency and internal policy compliance. An external audit is performed by an independent third party to provide objective assurance, certification, or regulatory evidence. External auditors follow defined standards and produce reports relied upon by regulators, customers, and partners. A concrete example: an internal security team may run quarterly configuration audits and adjust baselines, while an external auditor performs an annual certification review for ISO 27001 or a regulatory assessment for HIPAA. Misconceptions include assuming that internal audits replace external audits — they do not. Internal work reduces the risk of failures during external reviews, but external audits provide the independent attestation organizations often require. When planning audits, align internal audit findings to the external audit scope: document evidence, assign owners, and include remediation milestones so external reviews see a mature control environment rather than ad-hoc fixes. Ask yourself: does the evidence demonstrate sustained control operation or only a single point-in-time change?

Compliance frameworks provide structured approaches to identify and manage information security risk. Each framework serves different purposes. NIST Cybersecurity Framework is voluntary guidance organized into five core functions — Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, and Recover — and is useful for prioritizing improvements. ISO/IEC 27001 defines requirements for an information security management system and is the basis for certification to show an implemented, auditable program. GDPR and HIPAA are legal requirements for data protection in the EU and health data in the U. S., respectively; compliance means meeting specific privacy, protection, and retention rules. PCI DSS targets cardholder data environments and defines technical controls for payment processing. A concrete example: use NIST CSF to map gaps and prioritize mitigations, then adopt ISO 27001 to formalize the ISMS so you can produce certification evidence. A common misconception is treating frameworks as mutually exclusive; in practice they are complementary. Organizations often use NIST to structure risk management, ISO 27001 to show governance, and regulatory regimes like GDPR to define legal obligations. Effective auditors expect to see mapped controls, documented evidence, and how controls satisfy multiple frameworks where applicable.

Configuration audits verify that systems match an approved secure baseline. Baselines provide explicit settings for operating systems, network devices, applications, and databases. Consensus baselines such as CIS Benchmarks give practical, vendor-agnostic guidance to harden systems. A configuration audit workflow typically includes selecting the baseline, scanning systems with automated tools, reviewing deviations, and recording evidence of remediation. For example, a baseline might require SSH root login to be disabled and password aging parameters to be set; an automated scanner detects deviations and generates a report. Relying exclusively on manual checks is a common mistake because human reviews are error-prone and inconsistent across many systems. Instead, use automation and configuration management tools to enforce and periodically check desired state. Another misconception is that baselines are one-size-fits-all; they must be adapted to organizational context and justified for deviations. The key practical skill is being able to run a configuration scan, interpret deviations, assign remediation, and capture the before-and-after evidence that an auditor will accept. This continuous loop — enforce, scan, remediate, and verify — is how organizations maintain secure configurations at scale. Configuration Audits and CIS Benchmarks means use baselines like cis benchmarks with automated scanning and enforcement to detect and remediate deviations consistently.. In practical terms, baselines, automated scans, and why consistent configs matter. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The goal is to capture simple, verifiable outputs that demonstrate settings like password aging and SSH root login. These final key concepts summarize practical actions you must perform for compliant, auditable security. Configuration audits should use baselines like CIS Benchmarks and automated scans to detect and enforce desired state. Logs and audit trails must be centralized, time-synchronized, and retained according to policy; they are the primary source for detecting policy violations and reconstructing incidents. When findings appear, document them in a POAM with owners, milestones, and verification steps so auditors can see remediation progress. Avoid the trap of seeing audits as one-off checklists — instead, integrate auditing into continuous operations: automate enforcement, schedule recurring scans, and preserve evidence history. In practice, auditors look for reproducible commands, captured outputs, ownership of fixes, and verification evidence. Keep your remediation transparent and verifiable so compliance demonstrates both governance and operational control.
